unit.title: Apply knowledge of nail science to nail services

summary: This unit gives you the science behind every nail service: how the nail and the skin around it are built, how nails grow, the bones of the hand and foot, the germs that cause nail and skin infections, and what nail products contain and how they work. You will learn to analyse nails and skin, decide which conditions you can work on and which to refer, use products without harming the client or yourself, give a warm oil manicure for dry nails, and keep accurate records.

blocks.p: Every manicure, pedicure, nail enhancement and nail art service rests on the science in this unit. When you know how a nail is built and how it grows, you know why you must never cut live skin, why heavy filing ruins a nail, and why an injured matrix can spoil a nail for good. When you know the germs that live on hands and feet, you know why tools are cleaned and disinfected and why some clients must see a doctor. When you know what is in your products, you can use them safely and protect your clients and yourself from allergies, fumes, dust and fire.

This unit is mostly knowledge, but you use that knowledge with real clients. At every service you look at the nails and skin, decide whether the service can go ahead, choose the right products and method, and record what you found.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practical tasks you make a labelled poster of the nail and a chart of conditions to work on or refer, analyse a partner's nails and skin, make product safety cards from labels and safety data sheets, and give a warm oil manicure for dry nails. The assessor checks your knowledge, safety and judgement, not only the finished nails.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only hands, feet, products and the work area, never faces, and keep each partner's details private.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The nail and the skin around it

blocks.p: The nail is part of the skin. It protects the tip of the finger or toe, helps you pick up small things, and helps the fingertip feel. The nail plate together with all the living tissue around and under it is sometimes called the **nail unit**.

blocks.h: What the nail plate is made of

ul: The nail plate is made of **keratin**, a hard protein. Keratin is also in hair and in the top layer of the skin, but the nail's keratin is harder and more tightly packed.
The plate is built of many layers of flat, dead cells pressed tightly together. That is why a dry, damaged nail can split and peel in layers at the free edge.
The plate has **no nerves and no blood vessels**, so you can file it without pain. The living tissue under and around it has both.

The plate holds a little water and lets water pass through. After a long soak it swells and softens; as it dries it shrinks back. Products put on a nail that is still swollen from soaking can lift as the nail dries.
Calcium is **not** what makes nails hard. A nail holds only a very small amount of calcium; its hardness comes from keratin.

head: Part
Where it is
What it does and why it matters
rows: Matrix
Under the skin at the base of the nail, beneath the proximal nail fold.
Makes new nail cells: this is where the nail grows from
Has nerves and blood vessels
Its shape decides the shape and thickness of the nail. If it is badly injured, the nail may grow back ridged, split, misshapen or not at all
Lunula
The pale half-moon at the base of the nail. It is easiest to see on the thumbs and may be hidden under the skin on other fingers.
It is the front of the matrix showing through the plate. It looks paler because the new nail there is not yet fully hardened and clear. Pressure here presses on the matrix, so work gently.
Nail plate
The hard, visible part that you file and polish.
Protects the fingertip
Made of keratin; no nerves or blood vessels
Slides forward over the nail bed as it grows
Nail bed
The living skin directly under the nail plate.
Has many small blood vessels, so a healthy nail looks pink
Has nerves, so digging under the nail hurts
Fine ridges on it lock into the underside of the plate and hold it in place
Proximal nail fold
The fold of skin that covers the matrix at the base of the nail.
Protects the matrix. Its edge is the eponychium.
Eponychium
The living skin at the base of the nail, where the nail fold meets the plate.
Living tissue. With the cuticle it seals the base of the nail against germs. Never cut it or push hard on it.
Cuticle
A thin, colourless layer of dead tissue that comes from under the eponychium and sticks to the nail plate.
Dead tissue that can be loosened and removed from the plate. Removing it neatly helps polish and products stick; cutting into the living skin behind it does harm.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge, where the nail leaves the fingertip.
Seals the space under the nail against germs. Do not dig under the free edge with sharp tools.
Nail walls
The folds of skin along each side of the nail.
Protect the sides of the nail. An infection of these folds is called paronychia.
Nail grooves
The channels under the nail walls, along each side of the plate.
Guide the plate as it grows forward. Filing or cutting deep into the corners of a toenail can lead to an ingrown nail.
Free edge
The end of the plate that grows past the fingertip.
The part you shape. It is the oldest part of the nail and the most likely to split and peel.

blocks.note: The eponychium, the cuticle and the hyponychium are the nail's **seals**. If you cut live skin, push hard at the base of the nail or dig under the free edge, you break the seal: germs can get in and cause infection, and pressure on the matrix can damage the nail that grows next. Push back gently, remove only the dead cuticle from the plate, and never cut living skin.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: **Cuticle or eponychium?** The cuticle is the dead, colourless film stuck to the nail plate. The eponychium is the living fold of skin at the base of the nail. In a manicure you loosen and remove the cuticle; you only ease the eponychium back gently.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: What a healthy nail looks like

ul: A **pink** nail bed, showing a good blood supply. Press gently on the nail: the bed goes pale, and when you let go it turns pink again within about two seconds.
A **smooth**, slightly curved surface with no deep marks, spots or pits.
**Firm but flexible**: it bends a little and does not snap, split or peel.
An even free edge, and a plate firmly attached to the nail bed all the way to the tip.
A neat cuticle area, and soft, unbroken skin around the nail with no redness or swelling.

blocks.note: The pink comes from the nail bed, not the skin. On clients with brown or dark skin the nail bed may look a little darker, and many have one or more even, brown lines running down several nails that they have had for years. That is common and usually harmless. Compare with the client's other nails and ask how long it has been there (see 'Nail and skin disorders').
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A nail grows from the back, not from the tip. Cutting or filing the free edge does not make it grow faster or slower.

flow: The matrix makes new living cells
New cells push the older cells forward
The cells fill with keratin, flatten, harden and die
The hardened cells join the nail plate
The plate slides forward over the nail bed
It grows past the fingertip as the free edge

head: Fact
Typical figure
rows: How fast fingernails grow
About 3 mm a month (about 1 mm every 10 days).
How fast toenails grow
About 1 to 1.5 mm a month: roughly a third to a half as fast as fingernails.
Time to grow a whole new fingernail
About 4 to 6 months.
Time to grow a whole new big toenail
About 12 to 18 months.

blocks.note: These are averages, and every client is different. Use them as a guide when you tell a client how long a mark or a damaged nail will take to grow out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What changes the speed and quality of growth

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Age
Nails grow fastest in children and young adults and slow down with age. Older nails are often drier, more ridged and more brittle.
Warm weather
Nails tend to grow a little faster in warm weather.
The hand used most
Nails on the hand a person uses most usually grow a little faster.
Pregnancy
Nails often grow faster, and may become softer or more brittle.
Illness

A serious illness, a high fever, surgery or treatment such as chemotherapy can slow or briefly stop growth, leaving a groove across the nail (Beau's lines). Conditions such as anaemia, thyroid problems, poor circulation, diabetes and psoriasis can change how the nail looks or grows.
Diet and water
Nails need protein (to make keratin), iron, zinc, B vitamins and enough water. A poor diet can make nails thin, weak or ridged.
Medicines
Some medicines slow growth or change the colour or strength of the nails. Ask about them at the consultation.
Injury to the matrix
Can make the nail grow back ridged, split, misshapen or not at all. A knock to the plate alone usually just grows out.
Harsh treatment
Biting, picking, heavy filing, cutting the cuticle, frequent acetone and a lot of wet work weaken the plate. They do not change how fast the nail grows, but the nail breaks before it gets long.

blocks.note: Many clients believe white spots mean a lack of calcium. Most white spots come from small knocks to the matrix and simply grow out. Healthy nails come from a balanced diet with enough protein and water, gentle handling and moisture, not from one food or pill.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The skin and the bones of the hand and foot

head: Layer
What it is and what it holds
Why it matters in nail services
rows: Epidermis

The outer layer. It has no blood vessels. New cells are made at its base and move up; by the time they reach the surface they are flat, dead and full of keratin, and they are shed all the time. It also holds melanin, the pigment that gives skin its colour. It is thickest on the palms and soles.
It is the body's barrier against germs, water loss and chemicals
A cut that bleeds has gone right through it into the dermis
Dry, cracked skin lets germs and products in
Dermis
The thick living layer under the epidermis. It holds blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, oil glands, hair follicles, and fibres of collagen and elastin that keep the skin firm and stretchy.
Its nerves feel pressure, heat and pain: let them guide your massage pressure
Its blood vessels bring food and oxygen; warmth and massage increase the flow
Germs that reach it can spread into the blood
Subcutaneous layer
The fatty layer under the dermis. It cushions and protects the body, keeps in heat and stores energy.
There is little of it over the knuckles and the top of the foot, so bony areas need lighter pressure.

ul: **Sweat glands** (sudoriferous glands) in the dermis make sweat, which cools the body. The palms and soles have a great many. Feet that sweat in closed shoes stay damp between the toes, which helps fungi grow.

**Oil glands** (sebaceous glands) make sebum, the skin's natural oil. They open into hair follicles, so the palms and soles, which have no hair, have no oil glands. That is one reason hands and heels dry out and crack, especially with frequent washing.

blocks.p: The skin protects the body, feels touch, pressure, heat and pain, controls body temperature through sweat and blood flow, gets rid of some waste in sweat, and makes vitamin D in sunlight.

blocks.note: The skin is the client's barrier against infection. Never work over cuts, grazes or broken skin, never cut living skin, and treat any bleeding as a risk of infection (see 'Germs and infection control').
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Bones of the hand and arm

head: Bones
Where they are
How many
rows: Carpals
The wrist
8 small bones in two rows
Metacarpals
The palm
5 long bones, one leading to each finger and the thumb
Phalanges
The fingers and thumb
14: three in each finger, two in the thumb
Radius and ulna
The forearm
2: the radius on the thumb side, the ulna on the little-finger side

blocks.h: Bones of the foot and lower leg

head: Bones
Where they are
How many
rows: Tarsals
The ankle, heel and back of the foot
7, including the heel bone (calcaneus), the largest
Metatarsals
The middle of the foot
5 long bones, one leading to each toe
Phalanges
The toes
14: three in each small toe, two in the big toe
Tibia and fibula
The lower leg
2: the tibia (shin bone) at the front and inner side, the thinner fibula on the outer side

blocks.note: The **meta-** bones are the long middle bones: **metacarpals** in the palm, **metatarsals** in the foot. **Carpals** are in the wrist and **tarsals** in the ankle. **Phalanges** are the finger and toe bones in both.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Using this knowledge in a hand or foot massage

ul: Use firmer pressure on the soft, fleshy parts: the palm, the base of the thumb, the muscles of the forearm and calf, and the sole of the foot.
Use light pressure over bony areas: the knuckles, the back of the hand, the wrist bones, the top of the foot and the ankle bones.
Support the hand or foot with one hand while you work with the other. Move each joint gently, only as far as it moves easily, and stop if the client feels pain.
Take extra care with stiff or painful joints, for example from arthritis. Do not massage over a recent injury, a sprain or a broken bone, or over areas that are swollen, red or hot.
Make your long strokes towards the heart (from the fingers towards the elbow, from the toes towards the knee), the way the blood returns.

head: Movement
How you do it
What it does
rows: Effleurage
Smooth, even stroking with the palms or the flat of the fingers.
Starts and ends the massage, spreads the oil or cream, relaxes the client.
Petrissage
Kneading: pressing, lifting and squeezing the fleshy parts.
Works the muscles and increases the blood flow.
Friction
Small, firm circles with the thumbs or finger pads, for example round the joints and over the palm.
Warms the tissue and loosens stiffness.
Joint movements
Supporting the joint and gently circling the wrist, fingers, ankle or toes.
Helps keep the joints moving freely. Never force a joint.

blocks.p: **Micro-organisms** are living things too small to see without a microscope. Most are harmless and some are useful. Those that cause disease are called **pathogenic**, or **pathogens**. When germs pass from one person to another, directly or on tools, towels and surfaces, it is called **cross-infection**.

head: Type
What it is
Nail and skin examples
How it spreads
rows: Bacteria
Tiny single cells that multiply fast in warm, damp places. Some form spores that resist heat and chemicals.
Paronychia: red, swollen, painful skin at the side or base of the nail, sometimes with pus
Green or black patches under a lifted nail enhancement
Infected cuts and hangnails; impetigo
Touch, dirty tools, towels and foot spas, and broken skin.
Viruses
Much smaller than bacteria. They can only multiply inside living cells.
Warts on the hands, and verrucas (plantar warts) on the soles, caused by the human papilloma virus
Cold sores (herpes simplex)
Hepatitis B and C and HIV, carried in blood
Direct touch, shared tools and damp floors; blood-borne viruses through cuts and sharp tools.
Fungi
Moulds and yeasts. They grow in warm, damp, dark places, such as between the toes and under lifted nails.
Athlete's foot (tinea pedis): itchy, peeling, cracked or soggy skin between the toes
Fungal nail infection (onychomycosis, also called tinea unguium): thick, yellow or brown, crumbly nails
Ringworm (tinea corporis): round, scaly, itchy patches on the skin
Damp floors, foot spas, shared towels, files, socks and shoes.
Animal parasites
Tiny creatures that live on or in the skin.
Scabies: mites that burrow into the skin and cause an intensely itchy rash, often between the fingers and on the wrists.
Close skin contact, shared towels and bedding.

blocks.note: Warm, damp conditions help bacteria and fungi grow. That is why feet left damp between the toes, nails soaked for too long, towels left in a damp pile and moisture trapped under lifted products all lead to infection.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Level
What it does
Used for
rows: Cleaning
Removes dirt, nail dust, oil and product with detergent and water. It always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Every tool and surface, before disinfecting.
Disinfecting
A chemical kills most germs on hard, non-porous surfaces, if it is mixed as the label says and the surface stays wet for the full contact time. It does not kill every spore.
Metal and glass tools, the nail desk, finger bowls, foot spas.
Sterilising
Kills all germs, including spores, for example in an **autoclave**, which uses steam under pressure.
Metal tools that may have touched blood or broken skin, where the salon has an autoclave.
Antiseptic
Reduces germs on the skin.
Cleansing the client's hands or feet and your own hands before a service.

head: Item
What to do
rows: Metal pushers, nippers, scissors and metal files
Clean, then disinfect (or sterilise) after every client. Store in a clean, covered container.
Emery boards, paper-backed and foam files, buffers, orange sticks, toe separators, cotton, pads
Single-use. They are porous and cannot be disinfected: use new ones for each client, or give them to the client to take home.
Glass or crystal files
Can be cleaned and disinfected between clients.
Towels
A fresh towel for each client; used ones in a closed laundry bin; washed hot and dried fully.
Finger bowls and foot spas
Drain, scrub, rinse and disinfect for the full contact time after every client. Spas with jets or pipes also need the deeper cleaning the maker describes, because germs build up inside the pipes.
Products
Use pumps and dispensers, or take creams out with a clean spatula. Never dip a used tool or brush back into a shared product.

ul: Wash your hands before and after every client. Ask the client to wash hers, or cleanse her hands or feet with an antiseptic.
Cover any cut on your own hands with a waterproof plaster, and wear gloves when you may touch blood or broken skin and for pedicures where the salon's rules say so.
Wipe the nail desk with disinfectant and put out a clean towel before each client.

blocks.note: If a client bleeds: stop, put on gloves, press a clean pad of gauze or cotton on the spot until it stops, and offer a plaster. Clean and then disinfect or sterilise the tool, put bloodstained waste in a sealed bag, and record it. Never use a styptic pencil on more than one client; use a liquid or powder styptic on a single-use cotton bud.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Nail and skin disorders: work on, adapt or refer

blocks.p: A **disorder** is a change in the nail or skin that is not caused by germs, for example from an injury, the client's health or her habits. It does not spread. An **infection** is caused by germs and can spread. A **contraindication** is anything that means the service should not go ahead, or must be changed.

blocks.h: Conditions you can usually work on, with care

head: Condition
What you see
Usual cause
What you do
rows: White spots (leuconychia)
Small white spots or lines in the plate.
Small knocks to the matrix.
Work as normal. They grow out.
Ridges running from cuticle to tip
Fine raised lines along the length of the nail.
Age and dryness; very common.
Buff gently with a fine buffer; use a ridge-filling base coat. Do not file them flat.
Split, brittle nails with ridges (onychorrhexis)
Nails that split down their length and break easily.
Dryness, harsh products, wet work, heavy filing, age.
Oil manicures, cuticle oil daily, gentle filing, gloves for wet work.
Peeling nails (onychoschizia)
The free edge peels in thin layers.
Repeated wetting and drying; harsh products; filing back and forth.
Keep short; file in one direction; oil; gloves for wet work.
Bitten nails (onychophagy)
Short, uneven free edges; ragged, sore cuticles.
Nail biting, often a nervous habit.
Regular manicures, neat short shape, cuticle oil. Do not work over raw or bleeding skin.
Hangnails
Small splits of dry skin at the sides or base of the nail.
Dry skin; biting; cutting the cuticle.
Trim only the loose dead skin with clean, disinfected nippers; never pull it; oil. If red and swollen, refer.
Beau's lines
Grooves running across the nail.
Illness, high fever, some treatments, or injury to the matrix.
Work gently; they grow out. Refer if new and the client knows of no cause.
Bruised nail (haematoma)
A dark red, purple or black patch under the plate after an injury.
Bleeding under the nail after a blow or crush.
Work around it gently, with no pressure on that nail. Suggest a doctor if the pain is bad, the bruise is large, or the nail is lifting.
Stained nails
Yellow or orange plates.
Dark polish worn without a base coat; smoking.
Buff lightly; always use a base coat. Refer if the nail is also thick or crumbly.

blocks.h: Conditions to refer, or where the service must stop or change

head: Condition
What you see
Cause
Contagious?
What you do
rows: Fungal nail infection (onychomycosis)
Thick, yellow or brown, crumbly nail; may lift from the bed; often on toenails.
Fungus
Yes
Do not treat the affected nails or feet. Refer to a doctor or podiatrist.
Athlete's foot (tinea pedis)
Itchy, peeling, cracked, white or soggy skin between the toes; may spread to the soles.
Fungus
Yes
No pedicure. Suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Paronychia
Red, swollen, painful skin around the nail; sometimes pus.
Bacteria (sometimes yeast)
Yes
Do not treat. Refer to a doctor.
Green or black patch under a lifted enhancement
Green, then darker, staining of the natural nail where the product has lifted.
Bacteria (often Pseudomonas) growing in trapped moisture
Yes
Do not cover it or file it. Do not service that nail; refer to a doctor.
Warts and verrucas
Rough, raised lumps on the hands; flat, hard patches with tiny black dots on the soles.
Virus
Yes
Do not work over them. Suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Nail lifting from the bed (onycholysis)
The plate separates from the bed, usually from the free edge, and looks white or yellow there.
Injury, digging under the nail, allergy, fungus, psoriasis, some illnesses
Not in itself
If there is no clear cause or any sign of infection, refer. If it follows a known injury, keep the nail short and never clean under it hard.
Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia)
Thin, soft nails that curve up at the edges like a spoon.
Can be linked to low iron (anaemia) or other health problems
No
A gentle service only, and suggest she sees a doctor.
Ingrown nail (onychocryptosis)
The side of the nail grows into the nail wall; red, swollen and painful.
Cutting toenails too short or into the corners; tight shoes
No, but it can become infected
Do not cut into the corner. Refer to a doctor or podiatrist.
A new dark streak or spot
A brown or black line or patch that is new, single, widening or uneven, with no injury to explain it.
Can be harmless, but can be melanoma, a skin cancer
No
Do not cover it with polish or product. Advise her, calmly, to see a doctor soon.
Eczema, psoriasis or dermatitis
Red, dry, itchy, scaly or cracked skin; psoriasis can also pit the nails.
Not germs
No
If the skin is unbroken and calm, work gently with mild products. If it is broken, weeping or inflamed, do not work there; suggest a doctor.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor: do not name a disease or tell the client what she has. Describe what you have seen, in private and kindly, explain why the service cannot go ahead today, suggest who she should see (doctor, pharmacist or podiatrist), and write it on her record card. Then clean and disinfect everything she touched.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Melanoma can begin under a nail, and this type is the one most often found in people with darker skin. Bob Marley's illness began this way, under a toenail. Many clients here have harmless brown lines they have had for years; the warning signs are a line that is new, single, getting wider or darker, uneven, or spreading onto the skin around the nail.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: To prevent ingrown toenails, cut toenails straight across, level with the end of the toe, and only smooth the corners lightly with a file. Never cut down into the corners.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Nail products: what they are and how they work

blocks.p: Every nail product is a chemical. Know what each one does, how it works and what harm it can do, read its label and safety data sheet (SDS), and use it exactly as the maker says.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Solvent
A liquid that dissolves other substances. Acetone is a solvent for polish.
Evaporate
To turn from a liquid into a vapour (a gas) in the air.
Volatile
Evaporates quickly at room temperature, giving off vapour you can breathe in.
Flammable
Catches fire easily.
Monomer and polymer
A monomer is a small molecule. When many monomers join into long chains, they make a polymer.
Polymerisation (curing)
The chemical reaction in which monomers join up and the product hardens.
Adhesion
Sticking one thing to another.

head: Product
What it does and how
Safety points
rows: Acetone remover
A strong, fast solvent: dissolves polish, soak-off gel and acrylic.
Very flammable; vapour can reach a flame some distance away
Strips oils, so skin and nails dry out
Use a pump dispenser; small amounts; ventilate
Non-acetone remover
A gentler, slower solvent (often ethyl acetate). Used where the maker says acetone would harm tips or enhancements.
Still flammable
Still drying with frequent use
Cuticle remover or softener
Loosens dead cuticle from the plate. Many are strongly alkaline.
Keep it on the cuticle, off the surrounding skin
Rinse or remove it as the maker says
Cuticle oil
Softens the cuticle and keeps the nail and skin flexible.
Can trigger a reaction in clients allergic to an oil or fragrance in it.
Base coat and ridge filler
Helps polish stick and stops dark colours staining the plate. Ridge filler has fine particles that fill and smooth ridges.
Flammable; keep closed.
Polish and top coat
Solvents evaporate and leave a film of colour; top coat seals it, adds shine and slows chipping.
Flammable; use in a ventilated area.
Nail hardener or strengthener
Makes the plate stiffer. Some contain formaldehyde (it may be listed as formalin or methylene glycol).
Overuse can make nails brittle, and formaldehyde can cause allergy. Use only as the label says.
Dehydrator or nail prep
Removes surface oil and moisture before enhancements, so products stick.
Flammable; drying.
Primer
Helps enhancement products stick to the natural nail. Acid-based primers etch and bond; acid-free primers are gentler.
Acid-based primer can burn skin and badly damage eyes
A tiny amount, on the plate only
Eye protection if the maker says
Liquid and powder (acrylic)
Liquid **monomer** and powder **polymer** are mixed into a bead; it polymerises and hardens in a few minutes.
Strong vapour: ventilation and extraction
Keep off the skin: repeated contact causes allergy
Use only liquids made for nails
Gel
Gel is cured (hardened) only under the UV or LED lamp the maker says, by chemicals in it that react to that light.
Uncured gel on the skin, or under-cured gel, causes allergy
Use the matching lamp and cure time
Nail adhesive (glue)
Bonds tips and repairs in seconds.
Bonds skin too: keep off fingers and eyes
Acetone dissolves it

ul: Use the lamp the gel's maker names. Lamps give out different kinds and strengths of light, and a gel may not cure fully under another lamp.
Apply thin, even coats, cure each for the full time, and keep the fingers flat in the lamp. Cure thumbs on their own, so they sit flat.
Replace bulbs and keep the lamp clean as the maker says: old or dirty bulbs give less light.
Many gels leave a sticky film on top after curing, called the **inhibition layer**. It is normal for those gels: wipe it off with the cleanser the maker says. 'No-wipe' top coats do not leave one.
Some gels give off heat as they cure (a 'heat spike'). Warn the client; she may lift her hand out for a moment and put it back.

blocks.note: Never mix products from different systems or brands, such as one maker's primer under another's gel. They are made to work together, and a mixture may not set, may lift, or may harm the client.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use only liquid monomer made for nails, usually based on **ethyl methacrylate (EMA)**. Liquid based on methyl methacrylate (MMA) is unsafe for nails: it sets very hard, bonds too strongly, is hard to remove and can badly damage the natural nail. Never buy unlabelled bulk liquid.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Health and safety with nail products

blocks.p: **Overexposure** means contact with a product too often, for too long, or in too large an amount. Almost any product can do harm if exposure is high enough. Products get into the body in four ways: through the **skin**, by **breathing** vapour or dust, through the **eyes**, and by **swallowing** (for example from eating at the nail desk).

head: Point
Irritant contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis
rows: What it is
The skin is damaged directly by harsh products, solvents or a lot of wet work.
The body's defences become **sensitised** to an ingredient, such as the acrylates in gel and acrylic liquid, and react whenever it touches the skin.
How it starts
Gradually, where the product touches; anyone can get it.
Often after weeks or months of repeated small contacts. Once allergic, a person usually stays allergic for life.
Signs
Dry, red, sore, cracked skin, usually on the hands.
Redness, itching, swelling, tiny blisters or weeping skin round the nails and on the fingertips; sometimes on the face and eyelids, from touching them.
Who is at risk
Technicians who do a lot of wet work and remover work.
Technicians who touch products every day, and clients whose skin is touched by product or under-cured gel.

blocks.note: An allergy to acrylates can later stop a person from wearing any gel or acrylic nails, and can cause problems with some dental and medical treatments that use similar materials. Preventing skin contact is far better than dealing with an allergy.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Protect the client
Protect yourself
rows: Keep product off the skin: leave a small gap at the cuticle and sidewalls
Do not flood the nail
Cure gel fully with the matching lamp
Wipe off any product that touches skin before it is cured
Record any reaction and do not use that product on her again
Never touch product with bare fingers or wipe your brush on your fingers
Wear gloves (nitrile gives better protection than vinyl or latex)
Keep brush handles, dappen dishes and the desk clean
Close bottles after each use
Do not eat, drink or smoke at the nail desk; wash your hands before breaks

blocks.note: If a client's skin goes red, itchy or swollen during or after a service: stop, remove the product as the maker says, rinse with cool water, record what happened and the product used, and advise her to see a doctor if it does not settle. Never put more product on top.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Filing enhancements makes fine dust that you and the client can breathe in. Acrylic liquid, acetone and other products give off vapour.
The best control is **local extraction** at the desk: a unit that pulls vapour and dust down and away from both faces, at the source. Clean or change its filters as the maker says.
Keep the whole room well ventilated, with fresh air coming in and stale air going out. A fan that only stirs the air round the room does not remove vapour.
Wear a properly fitted dust mask of the type the SDS or the Centre says when filing enhancements. A paper surgical mask does not keep out fine dust well, and no dust mask stops vapour.
Wear safety glasses, and give the client some, when clipping tips, filing hard, or using primer.
Acetone, removers, polish, primer, dehydrator and acrylic liquid are flammable. No smoking or naked flames anywhere in the salon.
Keep only small amounts at the desk, in closed, labelled containers. Store stock in a cool place, away from sunlight, heaters, lamps and flames.
Put pads and wipes soaked in product into a **lined metal bin with a self-closing lid**, and empty it at least once a day into the outside waste.
Do not pour leftover acrylic liquid down the drain. Follow the SDS: often you soak it up in paper towel or mix it with powder so that it sets, bag it and put it in the closed metal bin.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat makes volatile products evaporate faster, so vapour builds up more quickly in a closed room, and heat and sun spoil products. Never store nail products on a sunny windowsill or in a hot car.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Labels and the safety data sheet (SDS)

blocks.p: The label tells you how to use the product, its main warnings and its use-by date. The **safety data sheet** gives the full facts. Read it before you use a new product, and keep the salon's SDS file where everyone can find it.

head: The SDS tells you
Example for acetone
rows: The hazards
Highly flammable; irritates the eyes; vapour may cause drowsiness
First aid
Eyes: rinse with water for several minutes; breathed in: fresh air
Fire-fighting
Which extinguisher to use; never water jets
What to do with a spill
Remove flames, ventilate, soak up, bag
Handling and storage
Closed, cool, away from heat and sun
Protective equipment (PPE)
Gloves; eye protection; ventilation
Disposal
As hazardous waste, following local rules

head: Route
What to do
rows: In the eye
Rinse with plenty of clean, cool running water, holding the eye open, for at least 15 minutes or as the SDS says. Get medical help for primer or any product that still stings.
On the skin
Wipe off, then wash with soap and water. Report a rash or burn.
Breathed in
Move to fresh air. Get medical help if the person has trouble breathing or feels unwell.
Swallowed
Do not make the person vomit. Get medical help at once and take the label or SDS with you.

sections.title: Analysing nails, choosing the service and keeping records

flow: Wash your hands; the client cleanses hers
Ask your consultation questions
Remove any polish
Look at one hand at a time, in good light
Check nails, cuticles and skin
Decide: work on, adapt or refer
Agree the service and record it

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: Her health: diabetes, circulation, arthritis, skin conditions, recent illness or surgery
Some conditions slow healing or reduce feeling, so cuts and heat are riskier; some need a doctor's advice first.
Medicines
Some cause bleeding more easily, thin or discoloured nails, or sensitive skin.
Allergies or past reactions
To avoid ingredients such as acrylates, latex, fragrances or certain oils.
Work, hobbies and home care
Washing, cleaning, gardening, typing and sport change which shape, length and service will last.
Past nail services and how they were removed
Enhancements and rough removal can leave the plate thin and weak.
Any problem she has noticed, and how long it has been there
A change that is new or growing needs more care than one she has had for years.

ul: **Nails:** shape and length; colour of the nail bed; thickness, strength and flexibility; ridges, spots, grooves or pits; peeling, splitting or lifting; bitten edges; staining; any dark streak.
**Cuticles:** dry, overgrown, torn or bitten; hangnails.
**Skin:** dryness, hard skin, cracks, cuts, warts, rashes, redness, swelling or heat.
**Feet:** also look between and under the toes, at the soles and the heels, and at the corners of the big toenails.

head: What you find
What suits the client
rows: Dry, brittle nails; dry cuticles
A warm oil manicure; a short, rounded shape; cuticle oil daily at home.
Peeling or splitting nails
Keep them short; file in one direction with a fine file; strengthening base coat as the maker says; gloves for wet work.
Ridges
Gentle buffing with a fine buffer and a ridge-filling base coat.
Bitten nails
Regular manicures to keep the edges and cuticles neat; a short shape; oil.
Thin, weak nails after enhancements
Give the nails a rest from enhancements; oil and gentle care while the damaged plate grows out.
Healthy nails
Any suitable service the client wants.

ul: Use a **fine** file on natural nails (around 180 grit or finer; finer still for weak nails). Coarse files (around 80 to 100 grit) are only for shaping enhancements.
File from each side towards the centre, in **one direction**. Sawing back and forth roughens the free edge and makes it split and peel.
Do not file deep into the corners at the sides: it weakens the nail and, on toenails, can lead to ingrown nails.
Never file or buff the top of the plate heavily. It thins and weakens the nail, and it does not grow back thicker.

blocks.h: Warm oil manicure for dry, brittle nails

flow: Check the hands for contraindications
Remove polish and shape the nails with a fine file
Warm the oil as the maker says, in a heater or a bowl of warm water, never over a flame
Test it on the inside of your wrist before the client's fingers go in
Soak the fingertips in the warm oil for a few minutes
Push back the cuticles gently and remove only dead cuticle
Massage the hands and lower arms with the oil
Buff gently with a fine buffer
Remove oil from the plates and finish with a ridge-filling base coat, or cuticle oil
Give aftercare advice and record the service

blocks.note: Oil left on the nail plate stops polish sticking. If you are going to polish, wipe the plates with remover before the base coat.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wear rubber gloves (with cotton liners if the hands sweat) for washing, cleaning and gardening.
Repeated wetting and drying swells and shrinks the plate and loosens its layers; detergents and bleach strip oils.
Rub cuticle oil into the nails and cuticles every day, and use hand cream after washing.
Keeps the plate and skin flexible, so they split and crack less.
Do not use the nails as tools to open cans or scrape labels.
Prevents breaks, splits and lifting.
Do not bite, pick or cut the cuticles at home.
Keeps the seal at the base of the nail intact.
Use remover only when needed, and a non-acetone one if the nails are dry.
Acetone strips oil from the nails and skin.
Eat a balanced diet with enough protein, and drink water.
The matrix needs protein and other nutrients to make healthy nail.
Wear sunscreen on the backs of the hands, and dry well between the toes.
Sun dries and ages the skin; damp skin between the toes lets fungi grow.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's name and contact details
09/11/2026, Paulette Harris, Port Antonio
Health, medicines and allergies
Arthritis in the hands; no known allergies
Nail and skin analysis
Dry, brittle nails; fine ridges; peeling free edges; dry cuticles; no contraindications seen
Service, products and method
Warm oil manicure; ridge-filling base coat
Any reaction or problem
None
Advice given
Gloves for washing; cuticle oil daily; keep nails short
Technician and client signatures
Trainee and client signed; checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, seen only by staff who need them. Never discuss a client's nails or health with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can name and label the parts of the nail and say what each one does.
I can explain the difference between the cuticle and the eponychium, and why the nail's seals must not be broken.
I can describe a healthy nail.
I can explain how a nail grows, give typical growth rates, and list what changes growth.
I can describe the three layers of the skin and the glands in the dermis.
I can name the bones of the hand, arm, foot and lower leg, and use this to massage safely.
I can describe bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, with a nail or skin example of each.
I can explain cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and say which items are single-use.
I can recognise common nail disorders by their medical names and say which I can work on and which I must refer.
I can refer a client tactfully without diagnosing.
I can explain what acetone, non-acetone remover, cuticle remover, hardener, primer, acrylic and gel do, and give a safety point for each.
I can explain overexposure, irritant and allergic contact dermatitis, and how to prevent them.
I can control vapour, dust and fire risks, and find facts on an SDS.
I can carry out a nail and skin analysis, choose a suitable service and give a warm oil manicure.
I can give aftercare advice and complete a record card.

blocks.note: In essays, explain the reason for each point. For example: 'I never cut the eponychium, because it is living skin that seals the base of the nail against germs.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The hard protein that the nail plate is made of.
The living tissue under the base of the nail that makes new nail cells.
The pale half-moon at the base of the nail: the visible part of the matrix.
The hard, visible nail; no nerves or blood vessels.
The living skin under the nail plate, rich in blood vessels.
The living skin at the base of the nail.
Dead, colourless tissue stuck to the nail plate at its base.
The skin under the free edge that seals out germs.
The folds of skin along the sides of the nail.
The channels at the sides of the nail that guide its growth.
The part of the nail that grows past the fingertip.
The outer layer of the skin; no blood vessels.
The living layer of skin with blood vessels, nerves and glands.
The fatty layer under the dermis.
The bones of the wrist / the ankle and back of the foot.
The long bones of the palm / the middle of the foot.
The bones of the fingers and toes.
A germ that can cause disease.
Germs passing from one person or object to another.
A machine that sterilises with steam under pressure.
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
White spots in the nail plate.
Grooves running across the nail, often after illness.
Split, brittle nails with ridges along their length.
The nail plate lifting from the nail bed.
Infection of the skin around the nail.
Athlete's foot: a fungal infection between the toes.
A wart on the sole of the foot, caused by a virus.
The liquid and powder of an acrylic system, which join and harden.
The sticky film some gels leave after curing.
Contact with a product too often, too long or in too large an amount.
A skin rash from contact with a product: irritant or allergic.
The maker's full safety information for a product.

c1.title: Gel polish before a wedding in Port Antonio
c1.text: Rochelle Mitchell, 29, a bank teller, books a gel polish manicure at a nail bar in Port Antonio the day before her sister's wedding. Trainee Sasha finds small white spots on two nails and fine lines running from the cuticle to the tip on both thumbs. Three days ago Rochelle shut her right middle finger in a car door: half of that nail bed is dark red-purple and it is still tender. The skin at the sides of several nails is dry, with small hangnails.

c2.title: Lifted acrylics in Linstead
c2.text: Keisha Brown, 24, comes to a salon in Linstead for an infill. Her acrylic nails were put on at another salon six weeks ago. Two have lifted near the free edge, and she has been gluing them down at home with nail glue. Under the lifted part of her left index nail, trainee Kerry-Ann sees a green-black patch on the natural nail. Kerry-Ann had already used a paper-backed file and a metal pusher on Keisha's other hand. The other nails look healthy.

c3.title: A farmer's pedicure in Christiana
c3.text: Mr. Desmond Walters, 58, grows yams and Irish potatoes near Christiana and wears rubber boots most days. His daughter has booked him a pedicure. He has diabetes and says his feet sometimes feel numb. Trainee Andrea finds the skin between his fourth and fifth toes white, soggy, peeling and itchy. His big toenails are thick, yellow and crumbly, and one corner of the left big toenail is red, swollen and digging into the skin.

c4.title: Fumes and sore fingers in Half Way Tree
c4.text: Four technicians do acrylic nails at a busy nail bar in Half Way Tree. One of them, Monique, has had red, itchy, cracked skin on her fingertips for a month, and her eyelids are puffy. She shapes her brush by wiping it between her fingers and does not wear gloves. The room has no extraction; a standing fan blows across the tables towards the door. Acetone is kept in an open jug on a sunny windowsill, and pads soaked in acrylic liquid go into a plastic bin with no lid.

c5.title: A warm oil manicure in Morant Bay
c5.text: Miss Iris Bennett, 72, a retired dressmaker in Morant Bay, has stiff, sometimes painful finger joints from arthritis. She still washes her clothes by hand. Her nails are dry and peel in thin layers at the free edge, and most have fine ridges. Trainee Shauna-Kay plans a warm oil manicure, followed by a hand massage.

questions.q: What should Sasha do about Rochelle's bruised middle fingernail?
o: File the plate thin over the dark patch so the blood can drain
Work around it gently, with no pressure on it, and record it
Refuse the whole manicure, as a bruised nail can spread to others
Cover the dark patch with an extra coat of gel to protect the bed
questions.why: A bruise under the nail (haematoma) is not an infection and does not spread, so the service can go ahead. Avoid pressure on the tender nail, never file into it, and suggest a doctor if the pain is bad or the nail starts to lift.

questions.q: Rochelle thinks her white spots mean she needs more calcium. What is the most likely cause?
o: Too little calcium in her diet over the past year
A fungal infection that is starting at the free edge
Small knocks to the matrix, which will grow out
Gel polish worn too often, which bleaches the plate
questions.why: White spots (leuconychia) usually come from minor knocks to the matrix and grow out with the nail. The nail's hardness comes from keratin, not calcium.

questions.q: How should Sasha deal with the hangnails?
o: Pull them off quickly so they cannot catch on the gel
Cut back the living skin at the sides below the hangnail
Leave them, then cover them with gel so that they lie flat
Trim only the loose dead skin with clean nippers, then oil
questions.why: Trim only the dead, loose piece with clean, disinfected nippers and soften the area with oil. Pulling tears living skin, and cutting live skin breaks the barrier and lets germs in.

questions.q: What do the fine lines running from the cuticle to the tip of Rochelle's thumbs most likely show?
o: Harmless ridges, often linked to dryness
Beau's lines left by a recent serious illness
An early fungal infection under the plate
Damage to the hyponychium from filing
questions.why: Fine lines along the length of the nail are common, harmless ridges linked to dryness and age. Beau's lines run across the nail, not along it. Buff gently and use a ridge filler; do not file them flat.

questions.q: What has most likely caused the green-black patch on Keisha's nail?
o: A bruise from the acrylic pressing down hard on the nail bed
Bacteria growing in damp trapped under the lifted acrylic
Mould spores carried in the acrylic powder from the other salon
Dye from the nail glue soaking into the natural plate
questions.why: Bacteria (often Pseudomonas) grow in the warm, damp gap under lifted product and stain the nail green, then darker. It is an infection, not mould or a bruise: do not cover it or service that nail, and refer her to a doctor.

questions.q: Why has gluing the lifted nails down at home made the problem worse?
o: Nail glue is food for fungus, so the patch will grow faster
The glue slowly thins the natural plate until it splits
It seals damp and germs into the gap under the acrylic
The glue stops the matrix from making new cells
questions.why: Gluing a lifted nail traps moisture, dirt and germs against the natural nail, which is exactly what bacteria and fungi need. Lifted enhancements should be removed or repaired properly by a technician.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do with the file and the metal pusher she has already used on Keisha?
o: Rinse both in hot water and keep them for Keisha's next visit
Wipe both with a dry tissue and store them in the UV cabinet
Soak both in acetone for an hour to kill any germs left
Bin the file; clean, then disinfect or sterilise the pusher
questions.why: A paper-backed file is porous and single-use, so it goes in the bin. Metal tools are cleaned to remove dust and debris, then disinfected for the full contact time or sterilised. Rinsing, wiping, acetone and UV cabinets do not make tools safe.

questions.q: Which of Mr. Walters' conditions could spread to the next client through a foot spa or a shared towel?
o: The peeling between his toes and the crumbly toenails
Only the red, swollen corner of the left big toenail
None of them, as foot problems do not pass between people
Only the numbness, which is caused by germs in his boots
questions.why: Athlete's foot and fungal nail infection are caused by fungi and spread through damp foot spas, floors and towels. An ingrown nail is not contagious in itself, and numbness from diabetes is caused by nerve damage, not germs.

questions.q: What should Andrea do?
o: Cut the ingrowing corner out deeply, then give the pedicure
Not treat his feet today, and suggest a doctor or podiatrist
Give the pedicure but leave out the foot soak and the massage
Put antiseptic cream between the toes, then carry on as booked
questions.why: Infection of the skin and nails, an inflamed ingrown nail and reduced feeling from diabetes all mean the pedicure should not go ahead. Explain kindly without diagnosing, refer him to a doctor or podiatrist, record it, and disinfect everything he touched.

questions.q: Why does Mr. Walters' diabetes call for extra care in any foot service?
o: Diabetes makes the toenails grow far too fast to be filed safely
Sugar in the skin makes polish and creams slide off the nails
Poor feeling and slow healing turn small cuts into big problems
Warm foot spa water can raise his blood sugar to unsafe levels
questions.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet. The client may not feel a cut or a burn, and wounds heal slowly and infect easily, so even a small nick can become serious. Ask whether his doctor or podiatrist is happy for him to have pedicures.

questions.q: Once his feet have been treated, which advice will help Mr. Walters most to keep the skin between his toes healthy?
o: Soak the feet in hot water every night for half an hour
Rub thick cream between the toes and leave it overnight
Wear the boots without socks so that the feet can breathe
Dry well between the toes; wear clean, dry socks daily
questions.why: Fungi thrive in warm, damp, dark places such as sweaty feet in rubber boots. Drying well between the toes and changing into clean, dry socks takes away the damp they need; long soaks and thick cream between the toes keep the skin soggy.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of Monique's sore fingertips and puffy eyelids?
o: Allergy from repeated skin contact with acrylic liquid
Dust from the files drying out the skin on her fingers
A fungal infection caught from one of her clients' nails
Air from the standing fan drying out her skin and eyes
questions.why: Wiping the brush on her fingers puts acrylic liquid on her skin many times a day, which can make her allergic (sensitised). Touching her face spreads it to the eyelids, where the skin is thin and reacts easily.

questions.q: Monique's cracked fingertips now bleed a little at times. Why does this put her more at risk?
o: Blood on her fingers makes the acrylic liquid set far too quickly
Broken epidermis lets germs and products reach the living dermis
Blood dries out the nail plate, so her own nails will lift
Cracked skin makes her sweat more, and sweat spreads fungus
questions.why: The epidermis is the skin's barrier. When it cracks deeply enough to bleed, germs and chemicals can reach the dermis, with its blood vessels and nerves. She should cover the cracks, wear gloves and see a doctor.

questions.q: Which change would do most to protect the technicians from vapour and dust?
o: A second standing fan to blow the air round the room faster
Air freshener spray every hour to cover the smell of the liquid
Extraction at each table that pulls vapour away at the source
Paper surgical masks for all staff, changed once a week
questions.why: Local extraction removes vapour and dust where they are made, before anyone breathes them in. Fans only stir the air round the room, air freshener hides the smell without removing anything, and surgical masks do not stop vapour or fine dust.

questions.q: How should the soaked pads and the acetone be dealt with?
o: Pads in the open bin, emptied weekly; acetone in a covered jug by the window
Pads burned out back each evening; acetone in an open bowl at each table
Pads put down the toilet; acetone poured into a labelled drink bottle
Pads in a lidded metal bin; acetone in a closed pump, out of the sun
questions.why: Pads soaked in flammable product go into a lined metal bin with a self-closing lid, emptied at least daily. Acetone is very flammable and gives off vapour, so keep it closed, in small amounts, labelled, and away from sun, heat and flames.

questions.q: How should Shauna-Kay file Miss Bennett's peeling nails?
o: In one direction, from side to centre, with a fine-grit file
Back and forth quickly with a coarse file to cut through the layers
Into a long, pointed shape to make the fingers look slimmer
Deep into the corners, so the sides of the nails cannot split
questions.why: A fine file used in one direction from each side to the centre seals the layers at the free edge. Sawing back and forth with a coarse file roughens the edge and makes peeling worse; a short, rounded shape suits weak nails best.

questions.q: During the hand massage, how should Shauna-Kay work over Miss Bennett's knuckles and finger joints?
o: Firm, deep kneading right over the knuckles to free stiff joints
Light pressure; move joints gently only as far as is comfortable
Pull each finger sharply until the joint clicks to loosen it
Skip the hand and massage only the forearm with firm strokes
questions.why: Knuckles are bony with little padding, and arthritic joints are often painful. Use light pressure over bones and joints, support the hand, move each joint gently within comfort, and keep firmer pressure for the fleshy palm and forearm.

questions.q: Why does washing clothes by hand make Miss Bennett's nails peel?
o: Soap and water add calcium to the nail, making it too hard
The water washes the keratin out of the nail plate each day
Wetting and drying swell and shrink it, so layers part
Handling cloth wears the nail bed thin under the free edge
questions.why: The nail plate takes in water and swells, then shrinks as it dries. Doing this many times a day, with detergent stripping the oils, loosens the layers at the free edge. Rubber gloves and daily cuticle oil help.

questions.q: A heavy pot fell on a client's big toe and the toenail came off. Roughly how long will a new big toenail take to grow all the way out?
o: About 4 to 6 weeks
About 3 to 4 months
About 12 to 18 months
About 5 to 6 whole years
questions.why: Toenails grow only about 1 to 1.5 mm a month, so a whole big toenail takes about a year to a year and a half. Fingernails grow about three times as fast and replace themselves in roughly 4 to 6 months.

questions.q: A gel has been cured for the right time under the right lamp, but a thin sticky film is left on top. What is it, and what do you do?
o: The inhibition layer: wipe it off with the maker's cleanser
Uncured gel from a faulty lamp: cure it again twice as long
Sweat from the client's hand: dry it with a towel and go on
A sign of allergy: remove the gel at once and refer the client
questions.why: Many gels leave a sticky inhibition layer where air touches the surface, even when fully cured. Remove it with the cleanser the maker says and avoid touching it, as uncured gel on skin can cause allergy. 'No-wipe' gels do not leave one.
